Lantern shell Laternula elliptica from Antarctic waters displays several remarkable life-history adaptations to the extreme polar environment. Field studies have revealed that the species attains a maximum shell length of 9 centimeters [Li = 9 centimeters], representing the ultimate size achieved after many years of slow growth in near-freezing conditions. The shell length at metamorphosis, when the free-swimming larva settles and undergoes transformation into a benthic juvenile, has been recorded as 0.06 centimeters , a diminutive size that reflects the substantial energy constraints operating at low temperatures. During the earliest stages of development, the newly hatched individual emerges from an egg measuring approximately 120 micrometers in diameter, which yields a calculated wet weight at birth of 0.0000009 grams [Wwb = 0.0000009 grams], a value derived from the spherical egg volume formula using a density of 1 gram per cubic centimeter. This extraordinarily small initial mass places the larvae firmly in the lecithotrophic category during their early planktotrophic phase, relying on endogenous yolk reserves before exogenous feeding on phytoplankton commences.

Laboratory rearing experiments conducted at a constant water temperature of 0.5 °C [T = 0.5 °C] have provided key insights into the species reproductive physiology. Under these controlled thermal conditions at 0.5 °C [T = 0.5 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged 15% [GSI = 15%]. Such comparative data highlight the evolutionary trade-offs between survival and reproduction that shape life-history strategies in extreme environments, where brief seasonal phytoplankton blooms impose tight windows for gamete production and spawning.

Longevity records for this species, maintained in aquaria at 0.5 °C [T = 0.5 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan spanning 5,110 days [am = 5,110 days], a duration equivalent to roughly 14 years that makes Laternula elliptica one of the longer-lived bivalves inhabiting the Southern Ocean. This extended lifespan is complemented by a correspondingly delayed onset of sexual maturation, with individuals reaching puberty at 1,095 days since birth [tp = 1,095 days since birth] under the same thermal regime of 0.5 °C at a temperature of 0.5 °C [T = 0.5 °C]. The three-year interval between hatching and reproductive maturity is remarkably protracted compared to temperate and tropical bivalves, which often mature within a single year. This slow pace of development is a direct consequence of the suppressed metabolic rates imposed by chronically cold waters, where enzymatic reaction rates and cellular processes operate at a fraction of their maximal capacity. The extended pre-reproductive period allows sufficient time for the accumulation of somatic tissue and energy reserves necessary to support successful gametogenesis at low temperatures.

The reproductive strategy of Laternula elliptica involves annual spawning events synchronized with the summer phytoplankton bloom, during which females release fertilised ova into the water column for external fertilisation. The gonadosomatic index reached 15% [GSI = 15%] at a temperature of 0.5 °C [T = 0.5 °C]. The veliger larvae that hatch from the yolk-laden eggs spend several weeks in the plankton, during which they feed actively on microalgae before reaching metamorphic competence. Upon settling, the post-larval spat measures just 0.06 centimeters  in shell length, a stage that represents a critical bottleneck in the life cycle due to high vulnerability to predation and physical disturbance on the soft sediments of the Antarctic shelf.

Understanding the physiological constraints shaping the life history of Laternula elliptica has implications for predicting its response to ongoing climate change in the Southern Ocean. The remarkably slow development from a wet weight at birth of 0.0000009 grams [Wwb = 0.0000009 grams] to a maximum size of 9 centimeters [Li = 9 centimeters] is governed by the strong temperature dependence of metabolic processes. Even minor increases in seawater temperature could accelerate the timing of puberty, which is currently set at 1,095 days since birth [tp = 1,095 days since birth] at 0.5 °C [T = 0.5 °C], potentially shifting the species phenology. However, the lifespan of 5,110 days [am = 5,110 days] at 0.5 °C might also be altered under warmer conditions, as elevated metabolic rates could accelerate senescence and reduce maximum longevity at a temperature of 0.5 °C [T = 0.5 °C]. The gonadosomatic index was 15% [GSI = 15%] at 0.5 °C [T = 0.5 °C]. The 0.06 centimeters  shell length at metamorphosis serves as a baseline for assessing whether warming alters larval survival and recruitment success in this keystone Antarctic bivalve.
